text: Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiast. Histor. l. III, c. 29, p. 357, ed. Vales. Amstelodami: Οὗτος ὁ Ἀναστάσιος πατρίδα τὴν Ἐπίδαμνον ἔχων, ἣ Δυῤῥάχιον νῦν προσηγόρευται, τήν τε Ζήνωνος βασιλείαν καὶ γαμετὴν τοῦ αὐτοῦ Ζήνωνος, τὴν Ἀριάδνην, ἐσοικίζεται. Idem ibidem paulo supra: Ἡ Ἀριάδνη Ἀναστασίῳ τὸν στέφανον ἐπιτίθησιν, οὔπω μὲν ἥκοντι εἰς γερουσίαν, ἐν δὲ τῇ λεγομένῃ τῶν Σιλεντιαρίων σχολῇ καταλεγομένῳ: ex quo, ut ex iis, quæ infra notabimus, apparet Anastasium obscuro natum loco. Silentiarii autem, observante Jacobo Goaro p. 35 et 36 notarum in Cedrenum, Græcis sunt ἡσυχοποιοί, id est, qui ad imperatoris latera silentium et quietem indicant, juxta Agathiam ἐπιστάται τῆς ἀμφὶ τὸν βασιλέα σιγῆς. V. et Fabrot. in Glossario Cedreni. Epidamnus vero, illius patria, erat ἐκ τῆς νέας Ἠπείρου ἐπαρχίας, ut ait Chronicon Paschale, de Anastasio videndum p. 329 et seqq.
anchorLine: γὰρ Ἐπίδαμνον ᾄδουσι (2) μὲν συγγραφεῖς, βοῶσι
en: Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History, book III, ch. 29, p. 357, Valois's edition, Amsterdam: Οὗτος ὁ Ἀναστάσιος … ἐσοικίζεται. The same, in the same place, a little above: Ἡ Ἀριάδνη … καταλεγομένῳ: from which, as appears from what we shall note below, Anastasius was born in an obscure place. The Silentiarii, as Jacobus Goarus observes on pp. 35 and 36 of his notes on Cedrenus, are among the Greeks ἡσυχοποιοί, that is, those who keep silence and quiet at the emperor's side, according to Agathias ἐπιστάται τῆς ἀμφὶ τὸν βασιλέα σιγῆς. See also Fabrot in the Glossary of Cedrenus. Epidamnus, however, his native place, was in the province of New Epirus (ἐκ τῆς νέας Ἠπείρου ἐπαρχίας), as the Paschal Chronicle says; on Anastasius see p. 329 ff.

text: Cangius Famil. Byzantin. p. 85: « Anastasii imperatoris patris nomen hactenus incertum manet apud scriptores: ex quibus duntaxat docemur, Dyrrhachio oriundum, ac religione Arianum fuisse... mater vero Anastasii Manichæa et soror fuit Clearchi Ariani, uti habet Theophanes, p. 117. Ex quo mirum videri haud debet, si hæreticis parentibus natus, toto regni tempore hæreticos ipsos (Eutychianos) tutatus, catholicos tam acriter insectatus sit. » V. Victoris Tunnunensis Chronicon, p. 325. De Anastasii parentibus vide et Theodor. Lector. Histor. Eccles. l. II, p. 558.
anchorLine: ξαιντο πατέρες νικᾶσθαι (6*). Ἐκ τοιούτων γὰρ
en: Cange, Familiæ Byzantinæ, p. 85: 'The name of the emperor Anastasius's father remains hitherto uncertain among the writers; from whom we learn only that he was a native of Dyrrhachium and an Arian in religion... but Anastasius's mother was a Manichaean and the sister of Clearchus the Arian, as Theophanes has, p. 117. Hence it ought not to seem strange that, born of heretical parents, he protected heretics (the Eutychians) throughout his reign and persecuted Catholics so bitterly.' See Victor of Tunnuna, Chronicon, p. 325. On Anastasius's parents see also Theodorus Lector, Eccles. Hist. book II, p. 558.

text:
Ἀνήγου σχῆμα· mallem ἀνάγουσα. Scilicet Anastasius, quod Baronium, Tillemont, le Beau, etc. fugit, antequam imperium adipisceretur, Antiochiæ episcopus non quidem consecratus, sed populi suffragiis electus et designatus fuerat. Theophanes in Chronographia, p. 116: Τούτῳ δ᾽ αὐτῷ ἔτει Πέτρος ὁ Γναφεύς (Antiochiæ episcopus) τέθνηκεν, καὶ προεβλήθη ἐπίσκοπος Παλλάδιος, πρεσβύτερος τῆς ἐν Σελευκίᾳ ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἁγίας πρωτομάρτυρος Θέκλης, συνεψηφίσθη δὲ Παλλαδίῳ καὶ Ἰωάννης ὁ Κωνσταντίνου, καὶ Ἀναστάσιος ὁ σιλεντιάριος ὁ κακῶς βασιλεύσας. Quæ ad verbum descripsit Cedrenus, p. 354, et sic e Theophane, ut omnia fere, convertit Anastasius Bibliothecarius in sua Historia ecclesiastica, p. 40, ed. Paris. ann. 1649, ed. Fabrotti: « Eodem anno, Petro Cnapheo mortuo, promotus est episcopus loco ejus Palladius, presbyter Leucensis (lege Seleuciensis) Ecclesiæ sanctæ primæ martyris Theclæ, cum quo ejectus est et Joannes Constantini, atque Anastasius Silentiarius, qui male posthac imperavit: » ubi pro ejectus emendo electus, cum textus Græcus Theophanis, quem semper κατὰ πόδα sequitur Anastasius Bibliothecarius, habeat συνεψηφίσθη, id est, simul electus fuit. Cl. Tillemont, qui Anastasium designatum fuisse Antiochiæ episcopum ignorabat, graviter lapsus est, hæc Theophanis verba sic vertens. Histoire des empereurs t. VI, art. 1, p. 532, Ed. Venet. 1739.: Anastase était à Antioche avec cette dignité (de Silentiaire en 448) lorsqu'il contribua à élever sur le trône de cette Eglise Pallade, Eutychien comme lui; scilicet per συνεψηφίσθη falso intellexit: suum calculum addidit, ut Palladius crearetur episcopus; cum potius significet, simul cum eo electus fuit. Idem Histoir. Ecclesiast. t. XVI, art. 51, p. 381, ed. Venet. 1732.: On mit en sa place (de Pierre le Foulon) Pallade, prêtre de l'église de Sainte Thècle à Séleucie, par la faveur de Jean fils de Constantin, et d'Anastase qui fut bientôt après empereur. Scilicet non assecutus est vim vocis συνεψηφίσθη, quam optime declaravit Cangius in suo mediæ Græcitatis Glossario, in Σύμψηφοι, quos dicit eos esse, qui populi clerique suffragiis simul ad episcopatum eligebantur seu proponebantur: nam ut fieri solet in ejusmodi electionibus, alii alium postulabant, inquit Socrates, l. v, c. 2; et l. vi, c. 11, tanquam τοὺς ἐπισκοπεῖν ἐπιτηδείους, ἢ προσδοκωμένους, ut loquitur Sozomen. l. VII, c. 3, donec, conspirantibus omnium suffragiis, unus eligeretur, vel e tribus ad principem delatis horum unus ad episcopatum provehetur; quod Cangius hoc ipso confirmat Theophanis loco, ubi observat tres hic συμψήφους appellari, licet plures forsitan essent; quod ex iis unum princeps, vel certe metropolita seligeret pro arbitrio; quippe, uti docemur e Novella 138 Justiniani c. 2, mortuo episcopo, coibant κληρικοὶ καὶ πρῶτοι τῆς πόλεως, ique, propositis sanctis Evangeliis, ἐπὶ τρισὶ προσώποις ψήφισμα faciebant, ὡς ἐκ τῶν ψηφιζομένων τριῶν προσώπων ὁ βελτίων χειροτονηθῇ τῇ ἐπιλογῇ καὶ τῷ κρίματι τοῦ χειροτονοῦντος. Qui quidem tres electi invicem, sive, ut horumce temporum Latini dicebant, suffraganei, σύμψηφοι et interdum etiam ὑπόψηφοι appellabantur, quemadmodum apud eumdem Socratem l. V, c. 5.: Συναγαγόντες τοὺς ὑποψήφους εἰς ἐπισκοπήν, εὑρίσκουσι τοὺς πάντας τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἕξ. In eumdem ac Tillemontius errorem inciderunt doctissimi Bollandistæ in Historia chronologica patriarcharum Antiochenorum, p. 90, col. 2, t. IV, Actor. SS. Julii, Ed. Venet. 1748, ubi sic loquuntur: « Hinc facile suspicari quis posset, imo deberet, non unum hic tantum electum esse patriarcham Antiochenum, sed tres eodem tempore. Verum hæc interpretatio omnino corrigenda est; neque enim Anastasius patriarchatum, sed imperium in ipsos etiam patriarchas tyrannicum affectabat atque aliquanto post consecutus est. Seduxit interpretem vox illa συνεψηφίσθη passive posita. Sed exempla non pauca grammatici proferunt, quibus tempus illud aoristum actionem significare ostendant. Sic igitur locus ille verti debuit: Palladio vero suffragatus est et Joannes, Constantini filius, et Anastasius Silentiarius (nomen est dignitatis, de quo vide Cangii Glossarium), qui postmodum pessime imperavit. Uterque autem in aula, cujus primi erant proceres, valebat plurimum; unde nihil mirum fuit, si, invitis haud dubie Catholicis, sedem illam Palladius obtinuit, quam tam potenti fultus patrocinio affectabat. »
Sic supra in adnotatione ad p. 8. observavimus, eosdem Bollandistas lapsos fuisse, cum inter CPolitanos patriarchas recensuerunt quemdam Macarium, qui nunquam patriarcha electus fuit, sed cum duobus aliis συμψήφοις imperatori, qui Philotheum prætulit, indicatus et propositus fuit. Eumdem autem Anastasium antequam imperium adipisceretur, patriarcha Euphemius, utpote hæreticum et Eutychetis sectatorem, e templo ejecerat. Theophanes et Chronographia p. 115: Εὐφήμιος δὲ ὁ ὀρθοδοξότατος Ἀναστάσιον τὸν σιλεντιάριον τὸν κακῶς μετὰ ταῦτα βασιλεύσαντα τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐδίωκεν, ὡς αἱρετικὸν καὶ ὁμόφρονα Εὐτυχοῦς, ἐνοχλοῦντα ὁρῶν· τὴν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ καθέδραν αὐτῷ ἀνέστρεψεν, ἀπειλήσας αὐτῷ, ὡς, εἰ μὴ παύσοιτο, ἀποκεῖραι τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοῖς ὄχλοις αὐτὸν θριαμβεῦσαι: ubi male Goar. Καθέδραν αὐτῷ ἀνέστρεψε vertit: eversa ejus in ecclesiæ cœtu sella; male etiam Anastasius Bibliothecarius, Histor. ecclesiastic. p. 48, hunc locum vertens, habet sedile ipsius, quod erat in ecclesia, subvertit: pejus etiam Cl. Tillemont Histoire des empereurs, t. VI, art. 1, p. 532, ed. Venet. Nihil autem clarius; hæc erat proprie cathedra in ecclesia erecta, in qua publice docebat et suos errores spargebat Anastasius. Suidas, qui voce Φατρία omnino videndus, eadem fere de Anastasio narrat: Ἀναστάσιος ὁ σιλεντιάριος ὁ μετέπειτα βασιλεύσας, ἐπὶ Εὐφημίου πατριάρχου Κωνσταντινουπόλεως καθέδραν κατασκευάσας, (cathedra sibi constructa) μετά τινων ἐφατρίαζεν, κ. τ. λ., de quo vide et Georgium Cedrenum, p. 353. Quæ quidem Suidæ verba male ibidem interpretatur summus homo, sed in quo accuratiorem Græcæ linguæ cognitionem desideres, Cl. Tillemont t. VI, art. 1, p. 532. Magnam autem pietatis speciem præ se ferebat acerrimus ille Catholicorum persecutor. Cl. le Beau Histoire du Bas-Empire, t. VIII, p. 310.: Anastase était dévot sans être chrétien; il allait à l'église avant le jour, et n'en sortait que quand le peuple s'était retiré; il jeûnait, il faisait de grandes aumônes. La multitude, toujours dupe de l'hypocrisie, admirait sa vertu. De quo vide Cedrenum p. 537, et Cl. Tillemont Histoire des empereurs, t. VI, art. IV, p. 537. Multas ecclesias Constantinopoli restauravit, referente Theodoro, Histor. ecclesiast. l. 2, p. 561. De hoc Victor Tunnunensis in Chronico, p. 326: « Messala consule, Constantinopoli, jubente Anastasio, sancta Evangelia, tanquam ab idiotis evangelistis composita, reprehenduntur et emendantur; » de quo adeunda egregia Petri Wesselingii Dissertatio. Sic eodem fere tempore, teste Evagrio Histor. Ecclesiast. l. III, c. 51, p. 361, multi sanctorum Patrum libri corrupti sunt; multi quoque Apollinaris libri sancto Athanasio et Gregorio Thaumaturgo falso ascripti sunt ab Hæreticis, hac fraude multitudinem in sui erroris societatem inducentibus. Anastasius autem, cujus pietatem hic tantopere prædicat Procopius, non solis Eutychianismi, sed et Manichæismi erroribus imbutus erat; de quo vide Cl. le Beau, Histoire du Bas-Emp. t. VIII, p. 450 sq.; Theophanem in Chronographia, p. 128. etc.
anchorLine: βοῶσα, καὶ πρὸς ἱερέως ἀνάγουσα σχῆμα (8)· καὶ
en: Ἀνήγου σχῆμα: I would prefer ἀνάγουσα. That is, Anastasius, which Baronius, Tillemont, Le Beau etc. missed, before he obtained the empire had been elected and designated bishop of Antioch, though not consecrated, by the votes of the people. Theophanes in the Chronographia, p. 116: Τούτῳ δ᾽ αὐτῷ ἔτει … ὁ κακῶς βασιλεύσας. Cedrenus copied this word for word, p. 354, and so, as nearly everything, from Theophanes, Anastasius Bibliothecarius renders it in his Ecclesiastical History, p. 40, Paris ed. 1649, ed. Fabrotti: 'In the same year, Peter Cnapheus having died, Palladius, presbyter of the church of Leuca (read Seleucia) of the holy first martyr Thecla, was promoted bishop in his place, with whom were cast out also John son of Constantine and Anastasius the Silentiary, who afterwards reigned badly'; where for ejectus I emend electus, since the Greek text of Theophanes, which Anastasius Bibliothecarius always follows word for word, has συνεψηφίσθη, that is, was elected together. M. Tillemont, who did not know that Anastasius had been designated bishop of Antioch, fell into grave error, translating these words of Theophanes thus (Histoire des empereurs, vol. VI, art. 1, p. 532, Venice ed. 1739): [French: Anastasius was at Antioch with that dignity (of Silentiary, in 448) when he helped to raise Palladius, an Eutychian like himself, to the throne of that Church]; he wrongly took συνεψηφίσθη to mean that he added his vote so that Palladius should be made bishop, whereas it rather signifies that he was elected together with him. The same, Histoire ecclésiastique, vol. XVI, art. 51, p. 381, Venice ed. 1732: [French: In his place (Peter the Fuller's) they put Palladius, priest of the church of Saint Thecla at Seleucia, by the favour of John son of Constantine and of Anastasius, who soon after became emperor]. He did not grasp the force of the word συνεψηφίσθη, which Cange best explained in his Glossary of Middle Greek, s.v. Σύμψηφοι, whom he says are those who were elected or proposed together for the episcopate by the votes of people and clergy: for, as usually happens in such elections, some demanded one, some another, says Socrates, book V ch. 2, and book VI ch. 11, as people fit to be bishops or expected, as Sozomen says, book VII ch. 3, until, all votes agreeing, one was chosen, or, of three brought before the emperor, one of these was advanced to the episcopate; which Cange confirms by this very passage of Theophanes, where he observes that three are here called συμψήφοι, though there were perhaps more; that of these the prince, or at least the metropolitan, chose one at his discretion; for, as we learn from Justinian's Novel 138, ch. 2, when a bishop died the clergy and first men of the city assembled and, the holy Gospels set out, made a vote on three persons, that the best of the three voted on might be ordained by the choice and judgment of the ordainer. These three elected, in turn, or, as the Latins of those times said, suffragans, were called σύμψηφοι and sometimes also ὑπόψηφοι, as in the same Socrates book V ch. 5: Συναγαγόντες … ἕξ. Into the same error as Tillemont fell the learned Bollandists in the Chronological History of the Patriarchs of Antioch, p. 90, col. 2, vol. IV of the Acta SS. July, Venice ed. 1748, where they speak thus: 'From this one might easily suspect, indeed ought to conclude, that not one only was elected patriarch of Antioch here, but three at the same time. But this interpretation must be wholly corrected; for Anastasius aspired not to the patriarchate but to tyrannical power over the very patriarchs, and obtained it some time later. The word συνεψηφίσθη, taken as passive, misled the translator. But grammarians cite not a few examples showing that this aorist signifies action. So the passage should have been translated: For Palladius there voted also John, son of Constantine, and Anastasius the Silentiary (the name of a dignity, on which see Cange's Glossary), who afterwards reigned most wretchedly. Both had great power in the court, whose chief men they were; hence it was no wonder if, against the will undoubtedly of the Catholics, Palladius obtained that see, which he sought supported by so powerful a patronage.' As we observed above in the note to p. 8, the same Bollandists erred when they counted among the patriarchs of Constantinople a certain Macarius, who was never elected patriarch, but was indicated and proposed to the emperor together with two others as συμψήφοι, the emperor preferring Philotheus. Now the patriarch Euphemius, as a heretic and follower of Eutyches, had cast this same Anastasius out of the church before he obtained the empire. Theophanes (sic 'et') Chronographia p. 115: Εὐφήμιος δὲ … θριαμβεῦσαι: where Goar wrongly translates Καθέδραν αὐτῷ ἀνέστρεψε as 'his seat in the assembly of the church was overturned'; Anastasius Bibliothecarius also wrongly, Ecclesiastical History p. 48, translating this passage, has 'overturned his seat, which was in the church'; Tillemont still worse, Histoire des empereurs, vol. VI, art. 1, p. 532, Venice ed. Yet nothing is clearer: this was properly the cathedra set up in the church from which Anastasius publicly taught and spread his errors. Suidas, who must be consulted s.v. Φατρία, tells nearly the same of Anastasius: Ἀναστάσιος ὁ σιλεντιάριος … κ. τ. λ. (cathedra sibi constructa, 'a chair built for himself'), on which see also George Cedrenus, p. 353. These words of Suidas the great man (Tillemont, vol. VI, art. 1, p. 532) interprets wrongly in the same place, though one would want in him a more accurate knowledge of Greek. This fierce persecutor of the Catholics bore a great show of piety. M. Le Beau, Histoire du Bas-Empire, vol. VIII, p. 310: [French: Anastasius was devout without being a Christian; he went to church before daybreak and left only when the people had withdrawn; he fasted, he gave great alms. The multitude, always the dupe of hypocrisy, admired his virtue]. On this see Cedrenus p. 537, and Tillemont, Histoire des empereurs, vol. VI, art. IV, p. 537. He restored many churches at Constantinople, as Theodorus reports, Ecclesiastical History book 2, p. 561. Of him Victor of Tunnuna in the Chronicon, p. 326: 'In the consulship of Messala, at Constantinople, by Anastasius's order, the holy Gospels, as having been composed by uneducated evangelists, are reproved and emended'; on which see Peter Wesseling's excellent Dissertation. So at about the same time, as Evagrius attests, Ecclesiastical History, book III, ch. 51, p. 361, many books of the holy Fathers were corrupted; many books of Apollinaris also were falsely ascribed to St Athanasius and Gregory Thaumaturgus by heretics, who by this fraud drew the multitude into fellowship with their error. Anastasius, whose piety Procopius here so loudly proclaims, was steeped not only in the errors of Eutychianism but of Manichaeism; see M. Le Beau, Histoire du Bas-Empire, vol. VIII, p. 450 ff.; Theophanes in the Chronographia, p. 128, etc.

text: Ἐρινὺν κοινήν. Sic apud Virgil. patriæ communis Erinnys. Hunc autem locum sic expressit Choricius oration. in Summum ducem apud Fabric. Biblioth. Græc. vol. VIII, p. 871: Οἶσθα τὸν νέον, ὃν ἐναγχός μοι συνέστησας, ᾧ γνώρισμα μέγιστον ὁ πατήρ. Οὗτος ἐμοῦ διηγουμένου ὅπως διένειμας τοῖς αὑτοῦ πολίταις τοὺς φόρους, ἀνέμνησέ με τοῖς περὶ σοῦ λεγομένοις Ἀριστείδου τοῦ Λυσιμάχου. Ἐκεῖνος τοῖς νησιώταις τάξας τὸ σύμμετρον, ἣν ἐπεδείξατο τοῖς Ἕλλησιν ἀρετήν, ταύτην ἔλαχεν ὄνομα· καὶ σὺ τῶν Ἀραβίων ἑκάστῳ τὴν ἐπιβάλλουσαν διώρισας οὕτω μοῖραν, κ. τ. λ., ubi legere mallem οὗτος ἐμοὶ διηγούμενος, quam ἐμοῦ διηγουμένου; nam hic juvenis ex Arabia redux Choricio narrabat quomodo Summus suis civibus Arabibus tributa solvenda descripsisset. In eadem oratione Pausaniam et Lysandrum memorat Choricius, quemadmodum et in hac Procopius. Uterque eodem modo veteres heroas collatos deprimit, ut suum extollat; uterque eodem modo historias et fabulas nihil ad rem facientes attexere amat. Denique facile agnoscitur Choricium sui præceptoris dicendi genus semper expressisse, illiusque orationes in suum succum et sanguinem convertisse.
anchorLine: Σὺ δὲ φόρους οὕτω μεγάλους, ὥσπερ Ἐρινύν τινα κοινὴν (47), μεταστήσας τῶν ὑπηκόων, τίνος
en: Ἐρινὺν κοινήν. So in Virgil, patriæ communis Erinnys ('the common fury of the fatherland'). Choricius expressed this passage thus in his oration against the supreme commander (Summus), in Fabricius, Bibl. Græc. vol. VIII, p. 871: Οἶσθα τὸν νέον … κ. τ. λ.; where I would rather read οὗτος ἐμοὶ διηγούμενος than ἐμοῦ διηγουμένου; for this young man, returned from Arabia, was telling Choricius how Summus had assigned the tributes to be paid by his fellow-citizens the Arabs. In the same oration Choricius mentions Pausanias and Lysander, as Procopius also does in this one. Both alike disparage the ancient heroes by comparison, in order to exalt their own man; both alike like to attach histories and fables that have nothing to do with the matter. Finally it is easily recognised that Choricius always imitated the style of his teacher and turned his orations into his own juice and blood. (Note continues onto p-0022 at 'Deni-|que'.)

text: Ἀπανθρώπους. Sic restitui pro ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπους, quod in cod. Cf. Cl. le Beau, l. XXXVIII, t. VIII, p. 348 seq. Tillemont, Histoire des empereurs, t. VI, art. IV, p. 538, ed. Quæ quidem potius referenda videntur ad hæc turpia spectacula, quæ ab Anastasio prohibita nullus alius auctor refert præter nostrum Procopium, sic paulo infra dicentem: Ἄρρενες γὰρ παῖδες, ὥσπερ τὴν ἰδίαν εἰς γυναῖκας ἀμειβόμενοι φύσιν... δῆμον ὅλον πρὸς ἀσελγῆ θέαν ἐκμαίνοντες κ. τ. λ. Sed Papæ Gelasii, Anastasio imperatori scribentis, verba sic se habent, p. 311, t. V editionis Conciliorum curatæ a doctissimis Nicolao Coleti, dignissimo doctissimorum Coletorum patruo: « Taceo quod pro rebus ludicris populares tumultus nunc etiam vestræ pietatis auctoritas refrenavit. » Unde cum non in hac epistola de rebus turpibus, ut ait Tillemont, sed duntaxat de ludicris agatur, hic a Gelasio respici puto populares illos tumultus, factiones imo et cædes, ob aurigas eorumque ludicra certamina in circo obortas, de quibus Cl. le Beau, ibid. p. 337. Cætera vide apud eumdem, p. 343 seq., ubi narrat horribilem in circo stragem ex hac causa derivatam, in qua 3000 homines trucidati sunt. Conf. eumdem p. 527 et 319.
anchorLine: θέας τινὰς ἦγον ἀπανθρώπους (48) αἱ πόλεις. Ἄν-
en: Ἀπανθρώπους. I have restored this for ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπους, which is in the codex. Compare M. Le Beau, book XXXVIII, vol. VIII, p. 348 ff. Tillemont, Histoire des empereurs, vol. VI, art. IV, p. 538, Venice ed.: [French: He removed from the public spectacles the combats of men against beasts; to which I think one can relate what Pope Gelasius writes, that he used his authority to restrain the people's mad passions for infamous things.] These words seem rather to be referred to those shameful spectacles which, forbidden by Anastasius, no other author reports except our Procopius, who says a little below: Ἄρρενες γὰρ παῖδες … ἐκμαίνοντες κ. τ. λ. But the words of Pope Gelasius, writing to the emperor Anastasius, run thus, p. 311, vol. V of the edition of the Councils prepared by the most learned Nicolaus Coleti, most worthy uncle of the most learned Coleti: 'I pass over that popular riots over theatrical matters your piety's authority has now also restrained.' Since therefore this letter deals not, as Tillemont says, with shameful things but only with theatrical entertainments, I think Gelasius here has in view those popular riots, factions and even killings arisen in the circus over charioteers and their theatrical contests, on which M. Le Beau, same place, p. 337. See the rest in the same author, p. 343 ff., where he tells of the horrible slaughter in the circus derived from this cause, in which 3000 men were killed. Compare the same, p. 527 and 319.

text: Προδιασκευάζων ἰνδάλματα. Sunt hæc prototypa ac exemplaria; atque ut Plinium secutus lib. XXXV, cap. 13 (ubi is tradit, Archesilai proplasmata pluris venire solita ab artificibus ipsis, quam aliorum opera), Græca voce notiori reddidi, proplasmata. Modellum vocant; et est futuri operis structa forma atque idea, cujus designatio summi Architecti est: aliorum artificum ut exsequantur, et in materiam inducant. Imagines, qui hæc vocet, non satis ex architecturæ rationibus loqui videatur; cujus hæc primis elementis Vitr. ascribit lib. I, cap. 2. Ubi Gulielmus Philander Castilionus potest videri. Auctor anonym. monstratum ab angelo imperatori in somnis τοῦ οἴκου τὸ σχῆμα, ait: quod non vetat, quin summi architecti fuerit singula designare, quibus ad illud Ædes σχῆμα in materia (formam scilicet) proveheretur.
anchorLine: τῶν τε γενη-|μένων προδιασκευάζων ἰνδάλματα (1). Καὶ μηχα-
en: Προδιασκευάζων ἰνδάλματα. These are prototypes and exemplars; and, following Pliny, book XXXV, ch. 13 (where he relates that the proplasmata of Archesilaus were wont to sell for more among the artists themselves than other men's finished works), I have rendered it by the better-known Greek word, proplasmata. They call it a model; and it is the structured form and idea of the future work, whose designing belongs to the chief Architect, that the other craftsmen may carry it out and bring it into the material. One who calls these Imagines would seem not to speak sufficiently from the principles of architecture; Vitruvius ascribes these to the first elements of it, book I, ch. 2, where Guillaume Philandrier of Châtillon may be consulted. The anonymous author, saying that the σχῆμα of the house (τοῦ οἴκου τὸ σχῆμα) was shown by an angel to the emperor in dreams, says: which does not forbid that the chief architect designed the particulars, by which the form of the building (its form, that is) might be carried into the material.

text: Τῷ τε γὰρ ὄγκῳ κεχόμψευται. Non putem docti esse interpretis, quod repræsentat Regia Lupara, Nam et nitore et proportione excellit. Scripserit et ipse mole; uti etiam reddit Arnoldus Vesaliensis, mole politum. Illud quoque excellit, minus est ad vim vocis, κομψεύεται: magisque elegantiam compositionis, et in ea præstantiam, ostendit.
anchorLine: τῷ τε γὰρ ὄγκῳ κεχόμ-|ψευται (2), καὶ τῇ ἁρμονίᾳ τοῦ μέτρου
en: Τῷ τε γὰρ ὄγκῳ κεχόμψευται. I do not think it the rendering of a learned interpreter, what the Louvre edition (Regia Lupara) gives: 'For it excels both in splendour and in proportion.' He too might have written 'by its mass'; as Arnold of Wesel also rendered it, 'polished by mass'. That 'excels' also is less to the force of the word κομψεύεται: and it shows rather the elegance of the composition, and the excellence in it.

text: Ὅθεν ἀεὶ διαγελᾷ πρῶτον ἡ ἡμέρα. Hic quoque mendo Luparæ, Unde dies videre semper incipit, pro, ridere, quod et emendatum inter varias lectiones. Non plene omnino Vesaliens. et ut metaphoræ vim satis reddat, Unde dies primum illucescit. Ipsa nota, in vere, in aere, atque hic in die, ex Theophr. De histor. plant. libr. VIII, 2, etc. Διαγελώσης τῆς ὥρας: vere jam adulto et tempore mitescente. Bud. Διαγελῶντος ἀεὶ τοῦ ἀέρος: Aere jam indulgente. Gaza. Hicque adeo: διαγελᾷ πρῶτον ἡ ἡμέρα.. Dies primum læta splendescit, aut quid simile parisque elegantiæ.
anchorLine: ἀεὶ διαγελᾷ πρῶτον ἡ ἡμέρα (3). Ὑπεραίρει γάρ, οἶμαι, τὴν γῆν ξύμπασαν (line read from the thumbnail)
en: Ὅθεν ἀεὶ διαγελᾷ πρῶτον ἡ ἡμέρα. Here too the Louvre edition has a fault, Unde dies videre semper incipit ('whence the day always begins to see'), for ridere ('to laugh'), which has also been emended among the variant readings. Vesalius does not render it fully, and does not give the force of the metaphor sufficiently: Unde dies primum illucescit ('whence the day first dawns'). The metaphor itself is from spring, from the air, and here from the day, from Theophrastus, Historia plantarum, book VIII, 2, etc. Διαγελώσης τῆς ὥρας: the spring being now advanced and the season growing mild. Budé: Διαγελῶντος ἀεὶ τοῦ ἀέρος: the air now indulgent. Gaza. And so here: διαγελᾷ πρῶτον ἡ ἡμέρα, the day first shines gladly, or something similar and of equal elegance.

text: Ταῦτα δέ, οἶμαι, γλώσσῃ. Ita mihi ex Vesalien. ipsoque paulo infra Procopio (λόγῳ φράσαι ἀμήχανον, hæc ipsa profitenti, impossibile ut sermone enarret) emendandum succurrit: ubi Hœsch. οἶμαι οὐδὲ γλώσσῃ: quod junctum τῷ, ἀμήχανά ἐστι, sensum facit ineptissimum; ipsum quem Mastretus reddidit, ac quo Procopius profiteatur, non esse impossibile aut valde arduum balbutiente lingua et impedita assequi, seu enarrare, ea, quorum tantis miraculum efferi; et quæ omnes facile spectatores in stuporem verterent. Quid si hiulca oratio, scripsitque Procopius, οὐδὲ νῷ ληπτὰ, καὶ γλώσσῃ. Ne mente quidem comprendi; ut vero lingua balbutiente et impedita, gracilique explicentur, impossibile esse. Sic sæpe cruces ligunt qui auctorum verba ac sententias truncant, unde vix se Lector expediat, fiantque illi vere ἀμήχανα, quæ ipsa ut ab auctoris calamo exierunt, erant εὐμήχανα: facilia et expedita; quorum exemplum nefastum edidere nuper Lugdunenses typographi, in Cursu theologico Joannis a sancto Thoma, theologi nostræ ætatis clarissimi, ac inter sancti Thomæ discipulos inclyti: non uno aut altero loco, sed fere sexcentis.
anchorLine: Ταῦτα δέ, οἶμαι, γλώσσῃ (4), τραυλιζούσῃ τε καὶ
en: Ταῦτα δέ, οἶμαι, γλώσσῃ. So it occurs to me to emend, from Vesalius and from Procopius himself a little below (λόγῳ φράσαι ἀμήχανον, these very words professing that it is impossible to relate in speech): where Hoeschel (has) οἶμαι οὐδὲ γλώσσῃ; which, joined to τῷ, ἀμήχανά ἐστι, makes a most absurd sense; the very sense which Mastretus rendered it, and by it Procopius shows that it is not impossible or very hard, with a stammering and hindered tongue, to reach or relate those things of which the miracle is brought out in such magnitude, and which would easily turn all spectators to astonishment. What if the oration is gappy, and Procopius wrote οὐδὲ νῷ ληπτὰ, καὶ γλώσσῃ (not graspable by mind, and by tongue)? 'Not even by mind to be grasped; that they be explained with a stammering and hindered and thin tongue is impossible.' So often those bind crosses who truncate the words and sense of authors, whence the reader can hardly extricate himself, and those become truly ἀμήχανα (impossible), which as they left the author's pen were εὐμήχανα: easy and ready; of which a nefarious example the Lyons printers have lately given, in the Cursus theologicus of John of St Thomas, a most illustrious theologian of our age and famous among the disciples of St Thomas: not in one or two places, but in nearly six hundred.

text: Παμμεγέθης ἐπανεστηκυῖά τις σφαιροειδὴς θόλος. Vocat anonymus νεωτερικὸν τροῦλον. Trullum vel trulum seu copulam, quæ temerarii ausus aliquid haberet: quod ejus brevi secuta ruina arguit, qua præcipua quæque angustæ illius domus comminuta; ipse scilicet altaris locus, et in eo sacra mensa, quæ ex omnium rerum fusilium speciebus miro artificio conflata, omni auro omnique genere lapidum pretiosior erat: ipsa una, mira concretione exsistens omnia. Soleas quoque et altari vicina loca et ornamenta, cancelli aliaque confracta, nulla deinceps Justini aliorumve principum munificentia, pro priore illa majestate, uni Magno Justiniano debita, reparanda.
anchorLine: τούτου δὲ τοῦ κυκλοτεροῦς παμμεγέθης ἐπαν-|εστηκυῖά τις σφαιροειδὴς θόλος (5), ποιεῖται: αὐτὸ διαφερόντως εὐπρόσωπον (read from the thumbnail; not checked in a 600 dpi crop)
en: Παμμεγέθης ἐπανεστηκυῖά τις σφαιροειδὴς θόλος. The anonymous author calls it νεωτερικὸν τροῦλον. Trullum, or trulum, or copula (dome), which would have something of rash daring: which the ruin that soon followed proves, by which every chief part of that narrow house was shattered: namely the place of the altar itself, and in it the sacred table, which, wrought with marvellous skill from the species of all molten things, was more precious than all gold and every kind of gem: itself one, existing as all things by a marvellous fusion. The soleae too, and the places near the altar, and the ornaments, the chancel-rails and the other broken things, no later munificence of Justin or other princes could restore, in place of that former majesty, owed to the great Justinian alone.

text: Ὡς ἀποσκοποῦντες πανταχόσε. Mastr. sequentem vocem, τὴν νοῦν, jungit particip. ἀποσκοποῦντες, cum palam, sicut et sequens, τάς τε ὀφρῦς cum sequenti jungenda sit, συννενευκότες: quas etiam conjunctio nectit. Significat vero auctor, quidquid videatur ex tantis illis spectaculis, aspectu stuporem injicere, sensumque ac superciliumvidentis detrahere, ut ex alio in aliud spectandi avidus semper digrediatur, nec artificium, quantum est, unquam assequatur. Hæc an velit novus interpr. lector viderit. Antiquus non satis feliciter exprimit.
anchorLine: ὡς ἀποσκοποῦντες πανταχόσε (6), τόν τε νοῦν τάς τε ὀφρῦς (anchor read from the thumbnail)
en: Ὡς ἀποσκοποῦντες πανταχόσε. Mastretus joins the following word, τὸν νοῦν, to the participle ἀποσκοποῦντες, whereas it is plain that, as also with the following, τάς τε ὀφρῦς must be joined with the following συννενευκότες: which a conjunction also ties. The author signifies that whatever is seen of those great spectacles throws astonishment upon the sight, and takes away the sense and the brow (confidence) of the beholder, so that, greedy to look, he passes from one thing to another and never grasps the art, however great it is. Whether the new interpreter wishes this, the reader may see. The ancient one does not express it happily enough.

text: Κεραννῦσα τὸν κόμπον τῷ κάλλει. Tribuit Lupara August. velut habeat κόσμον, ubi tamen æque κόμπον reperi: velit, parem cum elegantia magnificentiam: alterum artis subtilitas maxime præstabat, alterum materiæ pretiositas, aurum scilicet, variique generis pretiosissima marmora, nostro anonymo plenius exposita.
anchorLine: Χρυσῷ μὲν ἀκιδὸν ... κεραννῦσα τὸν κόμπον τῷ κάλλει (7)· νικᾷ μέντοι (read from the thumbnail)
en: Κεραννῦσα τὸν κόμπον τῷ κάλλει. The Louvre (Lupara) edition (and) Augustanus give it as if it had κόσμον, where yet I found κόμπον equally: he would mean magnificence equal to elegance: the one, the subtlety of art, chiefly furnished; the other, the preciousness of material, namely gold and marbles of every kind most precious, more fully set out by our anonymous author.

text: Καὶ τὰς περιστύλους αὐλάς. Columnatas aulas, quod reddit Mastretus, mihi satis durum. Alteram altera voce explicare voluit Procopius, suntque illi, quas ita vocat, ipse στοαί, seu porticus. Peristylia vocat Vitruvius, libr. VI, cap. 4, suntque vestibula, xysti, impluvia: Evangeliorum Latini interpretes reddunt, atria. Athenæus tradit, αὐλήν appellari perflabilem locum; et διαυλωνίζειν dici locum, utrinque ventum excipientem. Ab his locis subdialibus in quibus pro regiarum vestibulis prætorianorum excubiæ, regias ipsas dictas αὐλάς Menandro et Diphilo, auctor idem Athenæus: nobisque etiamnum sic vocantur. Priore duntaxat sensu Homerus usurpavit.
anchorLine: τὰς περιστύλους αὐλὰς (8), αἷς ὁ νεὼς περιβέβληται;
en: Καὶ τὰς περιστύλους αὐλάς. 'Columned courts' (columnatas aulas), as Mastretus renders it, seems to me rather harsh. Procopius wished to explain the one word by the other, and those which he so calls are themselves στοαί, that is, porticoes. Vitruvius calls them peristylia, book VI, ch. 4, and they are vestibules, xysti, impluvia; the Latin translators of the Gospels render it atria. Athenaeus relates that αὐλήν is called a place open to the wind; and διαυλωνίζειν is said of a place receiving the wind on both sides. From these open-air places, in which the praetorian guards keep watch in place of the vestibules of palaces, the palaces themselves are called αὐλάς in Menander and Diphilus, the same Athenaeus being the authority; and by us even now they are so called. Homer used it only in the former sense.

text: Χάλικας μικροὺς ὥσπερ ἀποξυσθέντες, ἀφίεσαν. De quibus hæc narrat Procopius, πεσσοὶ præcipue erant, seu pilæ illæ atque aggeres, quibus potissimum arcus illi majores nitebantur, uti paulo ante dixit de pilis fatiscentibus sub arcus onere ad Orientem oppositi: in pilis autem nihil calcis adhibitum aut cæmenti auctor Procopius, et ipse auctor anonymus; sed horum loco in petrarum lacunis liquatum plumbum: non ergo illis verbis columnas cæmentum dimisisse tradit, quod Mastretus reddit: Columnæ subditæ cæmentum perinde dimiserant, ac si quis eas distrinxisset, sed assulas, ut vocat Vitruvius, ac lapidum segmenta ex iis dissilisse; incrustationes μαρμαρώσεις, quibus parietes aliaque obducta erant, labefactatas esse. Id enim imminentis ruinæ indicium, ac vere laborantis fabricæ, nimio injecto molis pondere.
anchorLine: μικροὺς, ὥσπερ ἀποξυσθέντες, ἀφίεσαν (9). Καὶ
en: Χάλικας μικροὺς ὥσπερ ἀποξυσθέντες, ἀφίεσαν. Of which Procopius here tells: the πεσσοί were chiefly (the piers), that is those piers and embankments on which those greater arches mainly rested, as he said a little before of the crumbling piers, set opposite to the east beneath the burden of the arch: in the piers, however, no lime or cement was used, says the author Procopius, and the anonymous author himself; but in their place molten lead in the hollows of the stones: so he does not by those words say that the columns shed cement, which Mastretus renders: 'The underlying columns had shed cement, as though someone had scraped them,' but that splinters, as Vitruvius calls them, and fragments of stone flaked from them, (and) that the incrustations, μαρμαρώσεις, with which the walls and other things were covered, had been loosened. For that is a sign of imminent ruin, and of a fabric truly labouring, from the excessive weight of the mass thrown upon it.
